newsitem.title: KENYA: British minister surprised at Kenyan's comeback.
newsitem.headline: British minister surprised at Kenyan's comeback.

text.p: Britain's minister for Africa said on Saturday she was surprised Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi had restored his most controversial confidant to the cabinet.

"As far as Mr Biwott is concerned it is not for me to say who President Moi should put in his government. I can only say I was surprised," Overseas Development Minister Lynda Chalker told a news conference in Nairobi.

Nicholas Biwott was appointed a minister in the presidency on January 15, five years after Moi dropped him from the cabinet. Biwott was briefly detained in 1991 in connection with the 1990 murder of foreign minister Robert Ouko. He was released and no charges were pressed.
Chalker was replying to a question about Biwott's comeback which some western diplomats and foreign donors have condemned in private but not in public.
Chalker, the British government's Africa specialist since 1986, met opposition leaders on Friday and Saturday during her four-day visit to the former British colony.
Britain is Kenya's largest foreign investor and trading partner and the two countries also have close political and military ties.
Moi, vice-president George Saitoti and a host of ministers attended Friday's opening of Britain's new 10 million pound ($16 million) embassy in Nairobi.
Aged 72 and in power since 1978, Moi must call elections within the next year. The divided opposition is in the doldrums and accuses the government of loading the electoral dice.
"It is vitally important that all donors see these are the proper, free and fair elections they must be," Chalker said.
"There are obviously some problems with the I.D. (identity) cards. I.D. cards that are replaced by new ones should not then be able to be used by other persons," she said.
The opposition says the issuing of the cards is politically biased and a corrupt source of revenue for officials. Moi has extended the deadline for Kenyans to obtain cards until the end of February.
The opposition also complains that all broadcasting media are either state-owned or pro-government.
"There must be balanced access to the media for all political parties and that is something I have asked (Kenyan) ministers to turn their attention to now," Chalker said.
Asked if the opposition was already beaten, she said:
"I think they have made it more difficult for themselves to win, which doesn't mean they can't.
"I think they've got an uphill battle because there have been so many opposition voices."
Chalker implicitly denied the British government backed Moi and his ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU).
"I'm not on anybody's side except the side of the ordinary Kenyan people," she said.
